title: Tirana: Between Adaptation, Modernisation, Transition, and Difficult Heritage
content: Tirana provides a critical case for examining how accelerated post-socialist modernisation reshapes urban identity, heritage and the governance of land. The study combines a diachronic review of planning and architectural transformation with interpretive analysis of planning instruments, published research and morphological observations developed within the Tirana-Next programme. The findings indicate that verticalisation, iconic architecture and city-branding strategies selectively valorise strategic land while weakening the legibility of historical fabrics, socialist neighbourhoods, informal adaptations and socially productive open spaces. The demolition of the National Theatre (2020) and the 2026 current mobilisation concerning development in protected landscapes reveal a crisis of procedural legitimacy extending from urban heritage to territorial commons. The article introduces the selective privatisation of urban memory as a concept describing how institutional and market actors increasingly determine which histories remain materially visible. It concludes that modernisation should be reframed through differentiated conservation, adaptive reuse, neighbourhood-scale regeneration and meaningful public participation. Tirana's layered identity is not an obstacle to development, but a territorial resource and a precondition for socially accountable transformation.
